doc.title: Bruce Johnstone interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2013

title: Racial tension: brass knuckles, Harlem escorts, New York Mary
summary: He recounts being threatened in Copenhagen, bodyguards at Harlem clubs, and his fusion group New York Mary's album pulled from black radio when the cover showed white musicians.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was there any racial issues at the time, there?

Yes. I was threatened once on stage by a black guy who had some brass knuckles, and he came up screaming at me, “how dare you play my music?” And I think he was just there on vacation, but he’d had a little much to drink and all of a sudden he resented the fact that a white guy could play blues. And so the Danes kind of chilled him out. I think Dexter slowed the guy down too. But he was ready to take a swing at me because all of a sudden he thought that I was taking a cheap shot. But yes, there was some racial issues. Not in Denmark other than these guys who would come in. But yes, in the States there was, when I finally got here with Maynard. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-
Does it go under the heading of reverse?

I guess so. I guess, yeah. It’s just a very strange thing. I’d glad it’s kind of blown over. But at that time there was still factions and when I’d moved to New York, after I left Maynard, I would get calls from a couple of black clubs in Harlem and they would send somebody from the club to meet me at Grand Central Station and this guy’s job was to stick with me the whole time that I was there. He would drink with me, he’d hang out with me, he was very protective if anybody approached me, and then he would escort me back to Grand Central Station at the end of the gig. And it was a little unnerving.
It was a bit like being your bodyguard.

Yeah. So that was unnerving. And also I had started a fusion group called New York Mary, along with Rick Petrone and Joe Corsello. And we had two albums for Arista. And they did rather well. They were both “Hit Pick of the Month” in “Billboard” and “Cash Box,” and usually when they do that they say, you know, best track is — they listed all the tracks on both albums. So the second album Arista sent out in a plain cover, just as a promo. And it was getting airplay like crazy on all the black radio stations from Boston to Washington to Chicago. And then all of a sudden it got pulled. And it was because somebody showed up with the picture of five white guys on the front. And that was the feeling at the time.
You mean they were playing it but they didn’t know that you were an all white band.
I’d always thought that music really had no color and no barriers, but it did. Nowadays it’s so much easier.
